title: Care for detail, curdled into a fault
core: All of these describe attention to small details that has stopped being useful — but the words split on where the fuss is aimed. Three of them describe a standard you hold for yourself and what you'll accept; three describe an objection you press on someone else. That's the axis to fix first, because the GRE's sentences almost always supply a target (a host, a carburettor, a footnote, an opponent) rather than a definition. The second axis is blame: some of these can be earned praise, others are pure verdict on the fusser.

words.nuance: The standard is about what you will **accept** — cleanliness, quality, finish — not about anyone's error. It is the only word here that can carry physical squeamishness: the fastidious guest is repelled, not merely unsatisfied. Also the one that most readily flips to praise, because the fussiness is inseparable from real thoroughness.

The details guarded are points of **form** — protocol, ceremony, etiquette, procedure — never accuracy, cleanliness, or truth. Dignified where the others are petty, which is why it sits with diplomats and officers. Nobody is punctilious about a spreadsheet; they are punctilious about how the flag is folded.

The mildest and most domestic — an eye-roll, not a judgement, and about **preferences** rather than principles. Uniquely, it applies to objects and tasks: a finicky engine is temperamental and needs coaxing, a sense none of the others has. That inanimate use is the one the GRE reaches for.

The fuss is over **rules and learning**, and it is aimed outward at your mistake. Carries a specific charge the others don't: misplaced priorities plus display — the pedant is technically right, irrelevant, and pleased to be showing it. Always an insult; the identical behaviour praised is "rigorous."

The only one that indicts the **motive**: the objector wants you wrong, not the work right. Names a settled disposition rather than a single remark — you are captious all afternoon — and it is the most formal and most withering of the set.

The only **act** rather than a trait: a single small objection, or the making of one, with nothing implied about your character. And it alone runs polite — "my only quibble is the ending" concedes almost everything, a self-deprecating move no other word here can make.

exam_note: Watch the target noun: a person's standards (fastidious, punctilious), a machine (finicky), or another person's error (pedantic, captious, quibble) — and remember fastidious/punctilious can be compliments while pedantic/captious never are.
